source.title: Comparing Latent Concept Formation in State Space Models and Transformers via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Rithin Nagaraj; Rupa Laalasa Oruganti; Prerna Subhashchandra Kunder; Ashwini M. Joshi

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; minor PDF text-extraction artifacts do not prevent reading the results.
record.tranche_reason: It tests cross-architecture feature alignment with SAE co-activation Jaccard similarity, a different measure from the cited cross-architecture comparison method.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own cross-architecture Jaccard results and qualitative analyses of selected feature pairs. Its cited MPPC findings are not recorded as results. It does not sweep model scale or capability.
record.test_reason: The study compares SAE feature dictionaries of Mamba-130m and Pythia-70m-deduped by best-match binary co-activation Jaccard on a shared Wikipedia corpus. Its own results bear on whether features recur across architectures (V5). The method differs from the original sources, so it is T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. The authors find no SSM-specific 'dark matter': 99.98% of Mamba features align with Pythia features. They attribute this convergence to the statistical structure of the training data rather than to architecture, but they assert this rather than test it. They present the polysemanticity finding at the margins as hypothesis-generating, and acknowledge it may be confounded by the asymmetric SAE dictionaries.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE feature dictionaries and maximum pairwise binary co-activation Jaccard over a shared corpus; compares one Mamba and one Pythia checkpoint at one layer each. The paper contrasts this with cited MPPC work, but does not reproduce that method.
record.method_sensitivity: No alternative settings are tested. The paper notes that thresholds are empirical and the asymmetric SAE dictionary sizes may affect apparent alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors argue that Mamba compresses unrelated syntactic contexts into polysemantic features where Pythia keeps them separate, based on one pair. They say this is confounded by dictionary size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectures with a recurrent bottleneck show more polysemantic SAE features on formatting tokens than Transformers do.

record.problems: Only two model checkpoints, one selected layer per model, and one evaluation corpus are compared. The study uses asymmetric SAE dictionary sizes and acknowledges that the larger Pythia dictionary may inflate best-match alignment and the smaller Mamba dictionary may induce polysemanticity. Thresholds are descriptive and lack a null distribution; the polysemanticity analysis is a qualitative single-pair case study.

untested.parts: No sweep of scale or capability; one checkpoint per architecture.
No vision or paired image-caption data.
No comparison across seeds of the same architecture.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test.
Circuits; other model families, layers and sizes; symmetric SAE dictionaries; any null baseline.
Only one metric, one binarization threshold and one corpus, with no out-of-distribution inputs. The paper states that the thresholds are descriptive.

No plateau test. No test of shared data or objectives as the cause: the authors assert a data-manifold explanation but do not test it. Without a null, the Jaccard levels cannot show how complete alignment is.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 links and the V7 'supports' label are removed. The study does not test incompleteness, a plateau, or a data explanation: its Jaccard levels have no baseline, and the data-manifold claim is the authors' interpretation. The paper has internal inconsistencies: it reports 0.02% and 0.03% diverging, the categories leave a 0.25–0.28 buffer, and it calls the Grey and Alien features 'monosemantic' while also describing them as divergent. r3 and r7 describe the same feature.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep; the study compares one Mamba and one Pythia checkpoint.
No vision-language models or paired images and captions.
No comparison across random seeds of the same architecture.
No representation mapping, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping test.
Tests SAE feature co-activation correspondence for two model checkpoints at one layer each; it does not test circuits or broad recurrence across model families, seeds, or layers.
Uses one metric and one corpus; it does not vary similarity measure settings or input data, or test out-of-distribution inputs.
Measures alignment for one model pair, but does not test a scale-related plateau or causally compare shared versus differing training data or objectives.

rows.subject: Mamba-130m (aggregate over 12,288 features)
rows.operation_detail: Maximum Jaccard similarity to a Pythia feature, classified by the study's alignment threshold
rows.measure: Fraction and count of Mamba features with maximum Jaccard > 0.35
rows.note: Aggregate result over all Mamba features; the paper describes this category as strong alignment.
rows.check: No null or random-pair baseline. The 'Aligned' cut (J>0.35) was set after seeing the observed range of 0.234–0.411, so 99.98% describes a post-hoc partition. Even the best matches share under half their activation support. Activations were binarized at >0, and the Pythia dictionary is larger (32,768 vs 12,288), which the authors say may inflate matches. Remove the V7 link.

rows.value: J = 0.3415; described as firing on External LINKS headers at the ends of Wikipedia articles, with Strength: 4.19

rows.subject: Mamba-130m Feature 4454
rows.operation_detail: Maximum-Jaccard twin mapping and qualitative feature inspection

rows.note: The authors contrast this narrower trigger with the polysemantic Mamba feature.
rows.check: This is the Pythia side of the r8 pair and duplicates the same comparison. Its strengths are activation magnitudes, not alignment values. Remove the V7 link.
